newsitem.title: CHINA: Famine in N.Korea like time bomb, WFP official says.
newsitem.headline: Famine in N.Korea like time bomb, WFP official says.

text.p: Famine is ticking like a time bomb in flood-ravaged North Korea and could explode at any time, with the hungry eating bark, leaves and mushroom stems, a United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) official said on Monday.
"The situation is...a famine in slow motion," Tun Myat, director of the transport and logistics division of the WFP, told a news conference in Beijing after a two-week visit to North Korea.
"It's ticking away like a time bomb," Myat, a Burmese national, said.
Babies and children were in various stages of malnutrition and hospitals were bare of equipment and patients because people could not afford to send sick relatives for medical treatment, he said.
North Korea was devastated by unprecedented floods in 1995 and again in 1996, with entire crops wiped out.
The reclusive Stalinist state has been able to stave off famine only because its people have been eating alternative food, such as cakes made of bark and leaves.
"They ate barks and leaves," Myat said. "But not in the way that we would imagine anybody eating barks and leaves. It is done in a fairly...systematic way, fairly sophisticated way.

"Stalks of corn, cobs of corn, empty pea and bean pods, mushroom stems and whatever that in most other countries would either have been thrown away or would have at best been used for animal feed are now being milled into powder," he said.
The nutritional value of the alternative food is not known, and Myat said it was difficult to say when the "point of no return" would come.
In some areas, seaweed, a complementary food to the regular diet, had become a major staple, he said.

The WFP estimates North Korea needs 1.3 million tonnes of food to meet its basic needs in 1997. It has appealed for 200,000 tonnes of food worth $96 million, but has received only $38 million to date.
South Korea has pledged to give the rival North $6.0 million through the WFP this year.
The United States was the largest donor, giving $25.0 million. China, whose relations with the North were once described as "as close as lips and teeth", has pledged 70,000 tonnes of maize.
Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom have not followed up their donations last year with any pledges this year.
Pledges have been lacklustre due in part to skepticism of the North, which is still reluctant to open its doors to the outside world. A proud North has been reluctant to beg.
The level of agricultural activity was intense, Myat said. "Every scrap of land is being used," he said.
"If we have to grade them...I suppose one would have to give them an A plus for effort," Myat said.
North Korea saw light by the next harvest in October, but Myat said he was not optimistic.
A dearth of fertilisers and the hungry eating maize in green form could cut agricultural output, he said.
Forests have been burned down in many areas in the quest to increase arable land, but this would only make North Korea more susceptible to floods, Myat said.
North Korean provinces have been left to fend for themselves. Local authorities collect scrap iron and sell them to neighbouring countries, using the proceeds to buy food.

In another sign of the situation deteriorating, many people were seen riding on top of trains and travelling without permits in a country where movement is tightly restricted and travel permits are a must, Myat said.
